The human contribution shifts toward validating whether detected trends are substantive, spurious, or artifacts of data, methodology, or model behavior. This requires stronger contextual adjudication of unusual movements identified by automated processes.
justification: Trend identification in AI-supported validation settings requires understanding limits and biases of automated pattern recognition, which is not explicitly present in the current description.

description: Ability to translate recurring validation alerts, benchmark failures, and escalation cases into practical recommendations for improving collection, editing, compilation, and presentation methods.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of data and suggests possible feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures, and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.
change to work: Feedback and recommendations will now increasingly be informed by recurring machine-detected validation issues, quality-rule failures, metadata/paradata gaps, and escalation patterns. The role will contribute to improving methods not only from substantive analysis, but also from evidence generated by automated QA workflows.
justification: The role currently suggests feedback on methods, but future recommendations must draw on outputs from automated validation systems and exception analytics.

description: Knowledge of how automated validation rules, thresholds, escalation criteria, and data dependencies are structured and how they influence downstream output quality.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of data and suggests possible feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures, and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.
change to work: Feedback and recommendations will now increasingly be informed by recurring machine-detected validation issues, quality-rule failures, metadata/paradata gaps, and escalation patterns. The role will contribute to improving methods not only from substantive analysis, but also from evidence generated by automated QA workflows.
justification: To support recommendations, the incumbent must understand how validation logic relates to upstream survey and processing design, which is only implicitly covered today.

development area: Communication of automated quality assurance results
description: Ability to explain automated validation findings, escalation decisions, and quality implications in clear, non-technical language for internal and external users.
historic work: Key Activities - Provides data and assistance to users, within and outside Statistics Canada.
change to work: User assistance will expand to include explaining validation status, quality signals, and why certain outputs were escalated, delayed, or confirmed by human review. Users may also expect more timely outputs due to real-time validation, increasing the need for clear explanation of automated QA processes in plain language.
justification: The current role includes user assistance but does not explicitly require communicating machine-enabled validation outcomes or limitations to varied audiences.

description: Ability to contribute subject-matter interpretation to escalated validation cases and to support senior staff in reviewing whether automated findings warrant methodological or operational action.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in subject matter studies and reviews to support the work of project teams or senior officers.
change to work: Subject matter studies and reviews will increasingly incorporate evidence from automated validation systems, including repeated anomalies, benchmark deviations, and model-identified inconsistencies. The role will support project teams by contributing domain interpretation to these machine-identified issues and helping determine whether system logic should be adjusted.
justification: Current participation in subject matter studies does not explicitly require integrating findings from AI-enabled validation workflows.

development area: Translation of domain rules into digital validation requirements
description: Ability to express subject-matter expectations, acceptable ranges, and contextual conditions in a form usable by data engineers, methodologists, or system developers configuring automated validation workflows.
historic work: Technical Activities - Communiction - Liaises with other subject matter specialists and users to develop and translate subject-matter requirements into specifications for system development, to suggest improvements to ongoing programs, to negotiate procedural modifications and to establish project plans, priorities and target dates.
change to work: Liaison activity will increasingly involve communicating domain expectations that can be embedded into automated validation rules, benchmark logic, metadata requirements, and escalation pathways. The role will help translate subject-matter knowledge into machine-operable specifications for validation workflows.
justification: The current communication requirement references system development generally, but future-state work requires more explicit ability to translate domain knowledge into validation logic requirements.

description: Ability to describe automated validation logic, confidence, exception handling, and human review triggers in terminology understandable to operational staff, management, and users.
historic work: Technical Activities - Writes and presents detailed subject matter and technical concepts, definitions and terms in common terminology in order to explain and clarify divisional systems and applications.
change to work: Written and oral explanations will need to cover automated validation concepts, AI-assisted anomaly detection, and quality assurance logic in accessible language. This extends beyond traditional statistical concepts into machine-enabled validation processes and their implications for outputs.
justification: Current writing expectations do not explicitly include explaining AI-enabled validation processes to non-specialist audiences.

description: Ability to prepare guidance, procedures, and reports that document validation rules, automated checks, escalation protocols, and interpretation of machine-generated quality outputs.
historic work: Technical Activities - Writes program information manuals, training packages, monitoring procedures and management reports for use by colleagues, operational staff and management in the development, implementation and assessment of statistical programs.
change to work: Documentation responsibilities will expand to include automated validation procedures, exception-handling guidance, interpretation of machine QA outputs, and instructions for when human escalation is required. Monitoring procedures will become more digital and near-real-time.
justification: The current expectation includes documentation, but future materials must address automated validation operations and exception management, which are not explicitly covered.

development area: AI/ML methods in statistical quality assurance
description: Knowledge of how machine learning and automated analytics are used for anomaly detection, benchmarking, macro editing, and validation of statistical outputs.
historic work: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of statistical or economic theory and principles and the relevance of their application in a computerized environment, and the methods and techniques of data gathering, statistical estimation and economic modeling.
change to work: The phrase 'computerized environment' becomes materially more advanced, requiring familiarity not just with computer-based processing but with AI/ML-enabled validation methods, benchmarking logic, and automated quality assurance as part of routine statistical production.
justification: Current knowledge in a computerized environment is broad and may not cover AI/ML-specific validation approaches now embedded in the work.

description: Ability to use economic and social domain knowledge to assess whether machine-flagged output deviations are substantively credible, policy-relevant, or indicative of quality issues.
historic work: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of current and emerging economic and social issues relating to the program area in order to identify and assess trends and issues represented by statistical data series.
change to work: Domain knowledge remains essential but its use shifts toward contextualizing machine-detected anomalies and benchmarking results. The role must apply emerging issue awareness to determine whether divergences are plausible real-world developments rather than errors.
justification: Existing domain knowledge is still relevant, but future-state work requires applying it specifically within exception-based automated validation contexts.

description: Knowledge of factors that determine whether statistical outputs and processes are suitable for automated validation, including data standardization, metadata completeness, benchmark availability, and escalation design.
historic work: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of methods, techniques, practices and procedures to conduct studies and to develop/assess the feasibility and impact of new or modified statistical programs.
change to work: Assessment of new or modified programs will now need to include the feasibility and impact of automating validation activities, the suitability of available metadata/paradata, and the consequences of adopting exception-based review models.
justification: Program feasibility assessment in the current description does not explicitly account for automation-readiness of validation processes.

description: Knowledge of when to trust, question, or override machine-generated validation results, including the evidentiary basis for escalation and expert review.
historic work: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of the socio-economic concepts and methods to assess the validity of collected and processed data, the output from computer applications, the validity of database contents and results from alternative manipulations of data.
change to work: Assessment of validity extends from outputs of conventional computer applications to outputs from AI-enabled validation systems. The role must understand how automated checks affect judgments about validity and when human review should override machine findings.
justification: Current wording covers computer applications generally, but AI-enabled validation introduces specific issues around model behavior and override decisions.

description: Ability to use survey and population context to assess whether historical comparisons, external confrontations, and automated benchmarks are appropriate and meaningful.
historic work: Skills - 5. Contextual knowledge - Knowledge of the subject and universe of the survey is required in order to propose suitable changes to statistical or reporting methods and techniques.
change to work: Knowledge of the survey universe will now also support calibration of automated expectations, benchmark selection, and interpretation of anomalous output behavior across domains or populations.
justification: Survey-context knowledge must now be applied to tuning and interpreting automated validation, which is beyond the current explicitly stated use.

description: Knowledge of how differences in concepts, timing, coverage, and quality across internal and external data sources affect machine-driven benchmarking and confrontation results.
historic work: Skills - 5. Contextual knowledge - Knowledge of data sources within Statistics Canada in order to locate, analyze and compare related statistical output to ensure consistency and reliability
change to work: This knowledge becomes more important because automated validation increasingly confronts outputs with internal and external sources. The role must understand source comparability and limitations when assessing machine-generated consistency checks.
justification: While source knowledge already exists, future-state validation requires deeper understanding of comparability across sources within automated confrontation processes.

development area: Privacy and compliance in automated validation environments
description: Knowledge of confidentiality, privacy, and policy considerations related to using AI-enabled workflows, metadata, paradata, and linked quality checks in statistical validation.
historic work: Skills - 5. Contextual knowledge - Knowledge of the Statistics Act and other pertinent acts such as the Corporate Returns Act and Income Tax Act,  and of Statistics Canada policies  to ensure understanding and application in the collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation of data.  The position must have a particular awareness of the Statistics and Privacy Acts with respect to the security and confidentiality of data to ensure their own actions are in  compliance.
change to work: As validation becomes more automated and potentially more integrated across data sources and workflows, compliance knowledge must extend to the use of metadata, paradata, automated monitoring outputs, and AI-assisted systems in ways that preserve confidentiality, privacy, and policy compliance.
justification: Current compliance expectations are broad, but automated validation raises added requirements regarding responsible use of machine-enabled monitoring and linked quality information.

development area: Impact assessment of automated validation changes
description: Ability to evaluate how modifications to validation models, rules, thresholds, or digital workflows affect quality, comparability, timeliness, and downstream analytical use.
historic work: Responsibilities - 6. Research and analysis - Analyzes changes in procedures, methodology, computer technology and administrative services to determine the effect on data output, products and services.
change to work: The role will need to analyze how changes to automated validation procedures, AI models, thresholds, or monitoring tools affect outputs, comparability, timeliness, and quality. 'Computer technology' now includes machine-driven QA and validation engines rather than only general systems changes.
justification: The current analytical responsibility is relevant but does not explicitly require assessing impacts of AI/ML validation changes on outputs and services.

description: Knowledge of how automated validation assumptions, thresholds, training patterns, and benchmark dependencies constrain interpretation of results.
historic work: Responsibilities - 6. Research and analysis - Assesses and determines the impact and the constraints on results of the different concepts, definitions and conditions under which the data was collected, processed and stored.
change to work: This responsibility broadens to include assessing the constraints introduced by automated validation logic itself, such as model assumptions, benchmark dependencies, and sensitivity to changing collection conditions or data structures.
justification: Current expectations cover data conditions, but future-state work also requires understanding constraints introduced by validation models and automation logic.

description: Ability to identify where current workflows should be adapted to support automated validation, richer metadata capture, and efficient human escalation for ambiguous cases.
historic work: Responsibilities - 6. Research and analysis - Analyzes current collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures to ascertain their relevancy and to propose changes or alternative systems.
change to work: Analysis of methods and procedures will increasingly consider whether activities can be better supported by automated validation, how exceptions are routed to human review, and whether current processes generate the metadata/paradata needed for reliable machine QA.
justification: The current role analyzes methods and procedures, but the future state requires capability to assess and redesign them for AI-enabled validation environments.

description: Ability to critically assess, edit, and refine AI-generated narratives, summaries, and visual explanations so they accurately reflect statistical findings and methodological limitations.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of statistical program data and assists in the preparation of analytical material for internal use and publication purposes.
change to work: This activity expands from assisting with conventional analytical material to reviewing and refining AI-generated first-draft narratives, summaries, and visual explanations. The employee would need to check whether automated interpretations accurately reflect the data, methods, caveats, and intended audience, and then improve clarity and contextual relevance before internal or public use.
justification: The current work-description emphasizes participation in analysis and preparation of analytical material, but does not require capability to assess machine-generated interpretations for factual accuracy, bias, omissions, or overstatement.

development area: Operational understanding of LLM/AI output limitations
description: Knowledge of common failure modes of LLM/AI tools, including hallucinations, unsupported causal inferences, missing caveats, misleading emphasis, and inconsistency with source outputs.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of statistical program data and assists in the preparation of analytical material for internal use and publication purposes.
change to work: This activity expands from assisting with conventional analytical material to reviewing and refining AI-generated first-draft narratives, summaries, and visual explanations. The employee would need to check whether automated interpretations accurately reflect the data, methods, caveats, and intended audience, and then improve clarity and contextual relevance before internal or public use.
justification: The update introduces automated first-draft explanations and visualization outputs, which requires understanding of how AI tools generate narrative and analytical suggestions and where they may fail.

description: Ability to tailor AI-assisted and human-authored explanations of statistical outputs to technical and non-technical audiences while preserving analytical precision.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of statistical program data and assists in the preparation of analytical material for internal use and publication purposes.
change to work: This activity expands from assisting with conventional analytical material to reviewing and refining AI-generated first-draft narratives, summaries, and visual explanations. The employee would need to check whether automated interpretations accurately reflect the data, methods, caveats, and intended audience, and then improve clarity and contextual relevance before internal or public use.
justification: The updated process requires making results accessible and meaningful for varied audiences, beyond technical internal preparation alone.

description: Ability to verify whether AI-identified trends, anomalies, and explanatory patterns are supported by the underlying data, definitions, and production context.
historic work: Key Activities - Identifies statistical trends and developments.
change to work: Trend identification will increasingly be supported by automated analytics and AI-generated explanatory cues. The role now includes judging whether machine-suggested trends, drivers, or comparisons are statistically credible and substantively meaningful, rather than accepting automated pattern descriptions at face value.
justification: The current requirement covers trend identification, but not the evaluation of machine-generated pattern detection or explanatory statements.

description: Knowledge of the difference between description, association, and causation in statistical interpretation, especially when reviewing automated explanations.
historic work: Key Activities - Identifies statistical trends and developments.
change to work: Trend identification will increasingly be supported by automated analytics and AI-generated explanatory cues. The role now includes judging whether machine-suggested trends, drivers, or comparisons are statistically credible and substantively meaningful, rather than accepting automated pattern descriptions at face value.
justification: AI-generated explanations may blur descriptive, correlational, and causal interpretation; the role will need stronger discipline in distinguishing these forms of inference.

description: Ability to translate issues identified in AI-generated narratives or visualizations into actionable feedback on data production, metadata quality, and presentation methods.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of data and suggests possible feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures, and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.
change to work: Interpretation under 6.3 becomes more closely linked to upstream process quality. When AI-generated explanations expose inconsistencies, unexplained shifts, metadata gaps, or presentational weaknesses, the employee would be expected to feed those findings back into collection, processing, and presentation practices. This creates a stronger loop between output interpretation and methodological improvement.
justification: The current activity includes suggesting feedback to methods and procedures, but not using issues detected during AI-assisted interpretation as structured evidence for process improvement.

description: Knowledge of how collection, processing, editing, compilation, and presentation decisions affect the quality and explainability of final statistical outputs.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of data and suggests possible feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures, and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.
change to work: Interpretation under 6.3 becomes more closely linked to upstream process quality. When AI-generated explanations expose inconsistencies, unexplained shifts, metadata gaps, or presentational weaknesses, the employee would be expected to feed those findings back into collection, processing, and presentation practices. This creates a stronger loop between output interpretation and methodological improvement.
justification: Because automated explanation quality depends heavily on metadata and production context, the employee must better understand how upstream process choices shape downstream interpretability.

description: Ability to explain AI-assisted statistical narratives and visualizations to users, including confidence, limitations, caveats, and when further expert interpretation is needed.
historic work: Key Activities - Provides data and assistance to users, within and outside Statistics Canada.
change to work: User assistance will increasingly involve explaining outputs that have been prepared or summarized with AI support, clarifying what is machine-generated versus analyst-confirmed, and helping users interpret visualizations and narratives appropriately. This broadens the assistance function from providing data to mediating understanding of AI-assisted outputs.
justification: The current activity addresses user support generally, but not user-facing explanation of AI-assisted interpretations or communication of their limitations.

development area: Transparency and accountability in AI-supported communication
description: Knowledge of how to disclose, document, and communicate the role of AI assistance in interpretation while maintaining trust, clarity, and organizational standards.
historic work: Key Activities - Provides data and assistance to users, within and outside Statistics Canada.
change to work: User assistance will increasingly involve explaining outputs that have been prepared or summarized with AI support, clarifying what is machine-generated versus analyst-confirmed, and helping users interpret visualizations and narratives appropriately. This broadens the assistance function from providing data to mediating understanding of AI-assisted outputs.
justification: To support external and internal users responsibly, the employee must understand acceptable transparency practices around AI use in analytical communication.

description: Ability to enrich AI-generated interpretations with subject-matter context, caveats, and alternative explanations relevant to economic and social statistics.
historic work: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in subject matter studies and reviews to support the work of project teams or senior officers.
change to work: Subject-matter studies and reviews will now include assessment of AI-generated explanations as inputs to project work. The role will involve checking whether automated narratives reflect the substantive context and whether additional subject-matter analysis is required for sensitive or nuanced topics.
justification: The current role supports studies and reviews, but the update adds explicit need to supplement AI-generated drafts with domain context and nuance.

description: Ability to communicate subject-matter and business requirements for AI-assisted interpretation tools, including review needs, content safeguards, and output usability.
historic work: Technical Activities - Communiction - Liaises with other subject matter specialists and users to develop and translate subject-matter requirements into specifications for system development, to suggest improvements to ongoing programs, to negotiate procedural modifications and to establish project plans, priorities and target dates.
change to work: Liaison work will increasingly include specifying requirements for AI-assisted interpretation tools, such as accuracy thresholds, review workflows, escalation rules for sensitive outputs, and expectations for explainability and usability. The role may also need to communicate practical issues observed in AI-assisted interpretation to technical and methodological teams.
justification: The current liaison requirement relates to systems and procedures broadly, but not to defining user and subject-matter requirements for AI-generated analytical products.

description: Knowledge of review, escalation, and accountability structures needed to embed AI-generated narratives and analytics into statistical production safely.
historic work: Technical Activities - Communiction - Liaises with other subject matter specialists and users to develop and translate subject-matter requirements into specifications for system development, to suggest improvements to ongoing programs, to negotiate procedural modifications and to establish project plans, priorities and target dates.
change to work: Liaison work will increasingly include specifying requirements for AI-assisted interpretation tools, such as accuracy thresholds, review workflows, escalation rules for sensitive outputs, and expectations for explainability and usability. The role may also need to communicate practical issues observed in AI-assisted interpretation to technical and methodological teams.
justification: This is a cross-cutting gap because AI review workflows affect system design, analytical production, and user support simultaneously.

description: Ability to revise AI-generated explanations into clear, accurate, audience-appropriate language without losing statistical meaning or methodological nuance.
historic work: Technical Activities - Writes and presents detailed subject matter and technical concepts, definitions and terms in common terminology in order to explain and clarify divisional systems and applications.
change to work: This communication activity now includes translating AI-assisted analytical outputs into plain language while correcting ambiguities or inaccuracies introduced by automation. The employee must be able to preserve conceptual precision when simplifying machine-generated text for broader audiences.
justification: The current communication expectation covers technical-to-common language translation, but not editing AI-generated prose that may appear fluent while being conceptually weak or imprecise.

description: Ability to document workflows, review criteria, risks, and acceptable practices for the use of AI-generated narratives and visualizations in statistical programs.
historic work: Technical Activities - Writes program information manuals, training packages, monitoring procedures and management reports for use by colleagues, operational staff and management in the development, implementation and assessment of statistical programs.
change to work: Documentation duties would expand to include guidance on how AI-assisted interpretations are produced, reviewed, accepted, corrected, and monitored. Management reports and training materials may need to explain controls, responsibilities, and appropriate use cases for AI-generated explanatory content.
justification: Current documentation expectations do not explicitly include procedural guidance for AI-assisted analytical interpretation and oversight.

development area: Application of statistical theory in AI-mediated interpretation
description: Knowledge of how core statistical and economic concepts should be represented in AI-assisted narratives, and how to detect distortions or oversimplifications.
historic work: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of statistical or economic theory and principles and the relevance of their application in a computerized environment, and the methods and techniques of data gathering, statistical estimation and economic modeling.
change to work: This knowledge requirement must now extend beyond a general computerized environment to include AI-assisted analytical interpretation environments. The employee must understand how statistical and economic concepts can be misrepresented in automated summaries and how to correct them.
justification: The current knowledge requirement is broad and relevant, but it does not explicitly include AI-mediated interpretation risks in applying statistical and economic concepts.

description: Ability to use current economic and social context to question, refine, or reject AI-generated explanations that are incomplete, implausible, or insufficiently nuanced.
historic work: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of current and emerging economic and social issues relating to the program area in order to identify and assess trends and issues represented by statistical data series.
change to work: This requirement gains importance because AI-generated narratives may miss emerging context, overgeneralize, or misread the significance of developments. Human review must anchor interpretation in real-world economic and social conditions.
justification: The existing work-description already expects awareness of emerging issues, but future work requires stronger ability to use that context to audit and refine automated explanations.

description: Knowledge of methods for checking whether AI-generated explanatory content is faithful to source data, metadata, and validated results.
historic work: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of the socio-economic concepts and methods to assess the validity of collected and processed data, the output from computer applications, the validity of database contents and results from alternative manipulations of data.
change to work: The phrase 'output from computer applications' now extends materially to AI-generated narratives, visualizations, and analytical suggestions. Validity assessment must therefore include not only numeric outputs but also machine-produced explanatory content derived from them.
justification: The current requirement supports assessment of computerized outputs, but not specifically the validity of generated explanatory text and visualization narratives.

description: Knowledge of organizational policies, quality standards, and governance expectations governing the use of AI tools in statistical interpretation and explanation.
historic work: Skills - 5. Contextual knowledge - Knowledge of the divisional mandate, objectives, programs, policies and activities to adhere to the various statistical and administrative practices and procedures involved in the collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation of statistical data.
change to work: This contextual knowledge must now be applied to the governance of AI-assisted interpretation and explanation. The employee will need to ensure that the use of AI in explanatory outputs remains aligned with divisional standards, approved practices, and public communication expectations.
justification: This is a systemic gap because governance expectations affect all activities involving AI-assisted interpretation, communication, and documentation.

development area: Privacy and confidentiality controls for AI-assisted outputs
description: Knowledge of how confidentiality, privacy, and statutory obligations apply to the use of AI tools in generating and refining explanatory narratives and visualizations.
historic work: Skills - 5. Contextual knowledge - Knowledge of the Statistics Act and other pertinent acts such as the Corporate Returns Act and Income Tax Act,  and of Statistics Canada policies  to ensure understanding and application in the collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation of data.  The position must have a particular awareness of the Statistics and Privacy Acts with respect to the security and confidentiality of data to ensure their own actions are in  compliance.
change to work: AI-assisted interpretation raises additional compliance considerations, especially where prompts, generated narratives, or visual summaries may inadvertently expose sensitive information or reproduce disclosive detail. The role must therefore apply legal and policy obligations to AI-supported explanatory work, not only to raw data handling.
justification: The current requirement addresses confidentiality and compliance broadly, but AI-assisted narrative generation introduces new risk channels in prompt content, generated text, and visual explanation.

development area: Assessment of AI impact on analytical products
description: Ability to assess how AI-assisted interpretation affects quality, consistency, timeliness, accessibility, and risk in statistical outputs and user services.
historic work: Skills - 6. Research and analysis - Analyzes changes in procedures, methodology, computer technology and administrative services to determine the effect on data output, products and services.
change to work: The employee will now need to analyze the effect of AI-assisted interpretation technologies on analytical products and services, including changes to quality, speed, consistency, risk, and user understanding.
justification: The current analytical expectation includes computer technology changes generally, but not specific evaluation of AI impacts on interpretation quality and service delivery.

description: Ability to identify where AI-generated explanations fail to reflect conceptual definitions, collection conditions, processing limitations, or comparability constraints, and to correct them.
historic work: Skills - 6. Research and analysis - Assesses and determines the impact and the constraints on results of the different concepts, definitions and conditions under which the data was collected, processed and stored.
change to work: This analytical responsibility becomes more prominent because AI-generated explanations can overlook the constraints embedded in concepts, definitions, and data production conditions. The role must ensure those constraints are explicitly reintroduced into interpretation.
justification: Current analysis of conceptual and production constraints is relevant, but future work requires stronger skill in injecting those constraints into review of AI-generated explanatory text.

development area: Evaluation criteria for AI-enabled presentation methods
description: Knowledge of quality criteria for AI-assisted narratives and visualizations, including accuracy, interpretability, accessibility, transparency, and appropriateness for release context.
historic work: Skills - 6. Research and analysis - Analyzes current collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures to ascertain their relevancy and to propose changes or alternative systems.
change to work: Presentation methods now include AI-supported narrative and visualization generation. The employee would help assess whether these methods improve interpretability and accessibility, and where alternative processes or controls are needed.
justification: The existing requirement includes presentation methods, but future-state presentation increasingly includes generated explanatory content that requires dedicated evaluation criteria.
